notes: \cpara{An epigraph from H. Beam Piper's story ``Police Operation'' (\textsc{Astounding Science Fiction}, July 1948). In the story the saucers are real, antigravity landing disks from a spaceship, and the Paratime Police bury the true sightings under false reports.}
\cpara{Says that the author's disbelief in hidden aliens does not rest on the silliness of saucer cults, and hedges it: ``at least, I hope not.''}

\cpara{Applies the definition of evidence. Cults would arise whether or not there were aliens, so their existence is ``not much evidence one way or the other.'' The reasoning is correct, and the post names the one case, aliens suppressing cults, that would change it.}

\cpara{States the general principle in Pirsig's words. In the copy of \textsc{Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance} I could check, the line reads ``The world's biggest fool can say the sun is shining, but that doesn't make it dark out.'' It illustrates what Pirsig calls ``an old rule of logic that the competence of a speaker has no relevance to the truth of what he says.''}

\cpara{Argues that being reliably wrong would take knowledge of the truth, so fools are not reliably wrong. The arithmetic holds: reversing answers that are wrong 99.99\% of the time gives 99.99\% accuracy.}
\cpara{Restates the point as a joke about a broken engine.}
\cpara{Extends the principle from stupidity to evil, through the ``horns effect,'' which the post calls the converse of the halo effect.}

\clogic{The post gives no reason for ``how much less.'' By the paragraph before, reliable anticorrelation takes someone who knows the truth, and a deliberate liar does. The Stalin example that follows supports a narrower claim: an evil person is not wrong about everything.}
\cpara{The example: Stalin believed that 2 + 2 = 4, yet defending even that is read as taking his side.}

\cpara{The first corollary: argue against an idea's strongest advocates. The rule is old. John Stuart Mill, in \textsc{On Liberty} (1859), says one must hear the other side's arguments ``from persons who actually believe them; who defend them in earnest, and do their very utmost for them.''}
\cpara{People driven mad by an idea are no evidence against it; the example is New Agers and quantum mechanics.}

\cpara{The saying is John Stuart Mill's, in the House of Commons on 31 May 1866, in this form: ``I did not mean that Conservatives are generally stupid; I meant, that stupid persons are generally Conservative'' (Hansard).}

\clogic{True in the logician's sense: an attack on the speaker does not show the claim false. It does not make the speaker's record irrelevant. When a claim rests on the speaker's word, their reliability counts, as ``Argument Screens Off Authority,'' posted two days later, allows: there Arthur gives a delinquent's flat assertion 10\% and a geologist's 90\%, and the post calls this taking ``the speaker's authority into account.''}
\cpara{An argument against genocide should not depend on who advocated it.}
\cpara{Credits Robin Hanson with the idea that willingness to believe follows willingness to affiliate with believers; the example is reluctance to side with ``strident'' atheists.}
\cpara{A failed system does not show that each of its parts is at fault.}
\cpara{The last corollary turns the title on methods: reversing a failed approach is unlikely to find the one that works.}
